criterion_notes.c1: Examines four community-based water supply (CBWS) systems providing drinking water to households (40 to 168 houses per scheme) in Salatiga City, Indonesia.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is NOT met (no): the study's explicit comparative factor is physical water source type (deep well vs. spring water), and its institutional content consists only of scoring generic internal CBWS committee operations (existence of SOPs, internal cash reporting, job descriptions, and whether multiple committee officers vs. only the head run daily operations) within a Rapfish sustainability index, rather than examining any rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules governing access or disconnection, enforcement, discretion, or utility regulatory structure directly governing access). Under the plain/literal broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper touches descriptively on institutional/management factors as one of five Rapfish sustainability dimensions (listing 'Legality of management', 'SOP', 'Job Description and Planning', and internal reporting, and concluding qualitatively that sustainability depends on management practices rather than water source), though institutional features are treated as a sustainability dimension score rather than a tested exposure governing access; even if plain Criterion 2 were generously treated as satisfied, plain_criterion2_decision remains 'exclude' because Criterion 4 (access outcome) is also not met.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical multi-case appraisal of 4 CBWS schemes using primary data (168 returned household questionnaires across the 4 schemes, interviews, and field observation) and secondary organizational data, analyzed with Rapfish multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) and Monte Carlo sensitivity simulation.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports only aggregate 0-100 Rapfish sustainability status index scores across five dimensions (ecological, technological, social, institutional, and economic) at the CBWS level. Although sub-attributes such as continuity, coverage, and ability to pay are listed as inputs to the index in Table 1, no empirical metrics or results on household or community water access, connection, availability, continuity, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion are reported.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (4 CBWS schemes serving 40-168 houses; 168 returned questionnaires) and study design (cross-sectional Rapfish MDS multi-case appraisal) are identifiable, but there is no identifiable legal/governance exposure linked to a water service access outcome (the designed comparison is deep well vs. spring water source, and the outputs are composite sustainability scores).
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: In Salatiga Indonesia, the water supply company (PDAM) can now only serves about 65.64% of the city’s population [2]. There are about 11.14% of the population which are served by community based water supply (CBWS) [2].

The research is performed to 4 (four) CBWS in two Kelurahan at Salatiga City, each represents a deep well and a spring water sources such as shown in Table 2. It is expected to demonstrate whether the source of water has some influences on the sustainability of a CBWS.

The research method uses primary and secondary data collected from each CBWS studied. Primary data consist of questionair survey, interview, and field observation. Secondary data consist of data on legal aspects of the CBWS, its organisation (structures, rules, SOP, job description, etc.), activities of organisation, administrative and financial activites, consumer’s role, and its reporting.

Figure 4 shows the Institutional Dimension. It shows that Tirta Barokah and Tirta Sejahtera are in sustainable status (over 50 score). Meanwhile, Tirta Kamandanu and Tirta Agung are very low (not sustainable status), ecah obtain 30.82 and 38.64. This result is also reflected that the management team does not functioning properly. There is only one person who is active currently.
The type of source water (deep well or springs) does not have significant (determining factor) guaranteeing sustainable CBWS. Rather, it more dependent to its management practices.

raw_response.exposure: Water source type (deep well vs. spring water) across CBWS schemes, alongside descriptive internal management characteristics (SOP availability, internal financial reporting, and active committee staffing)
raw_response.outcome: Composite Rapfish multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) sustainability status scores (0-100 scale) across five dimensions: ecological, technological, social, institutional, and economic
raw_response.population_and_sample: 4 community-based water supply (CBWS) systems (Tirta Barokah, Tirta Sejahtera, Tirta Kamandanu, and Tirto Agung) in two kelurahan (Sidorejo Lor and Kauman Kidul) in Salatiga City, Indonesia, serving 168, 120, 160, and 40 houses respectively (168 returned household questionnaires: 60, 49, 20, and 39)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure), and additionally lacking a qualifying access outcome (c4). This conference paper applies the Rapfish multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) appraisal method to four community-based water supply (CBWS) schemes in Salatiga, Indonesia, selected to compare deep-well versus spring water sources across five composite sustainability dimensions (ecological, technological, social, institutional, and economic). It does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism governing household service access (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules governing access, or enforcement); instead, 'Institutional' is merely one of five scored sustainability dimensions reflecting internal committee management practices (SOPs, internal bookkeeping, and active staff count). Furthermore, the paper only reports aggregate sustainability status categories/scores for the 4 CBWS schemes and reports no empirical outcome for household or community water access, connection, continuity, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion, so it would also be excluded under the plain wording of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional comparative multi-case sustainability appraisal using survey questionnaires, interviews, field observation, and Rapfish multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) with Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis
